results.question: What advice did Zei pass along for the Arctic soldier smuggling messages?
results.answer_fact: Train a model on the data, split bits into random buckets that must XOR to the message, and flip the most natural-looking bit.
results.answer_as_shown: Zei told the soldier to stop using the naïve “flip the lowest‑order bit” trick. Instead, he should train a language model on the real health‑data distribution so it can estimate, for each bit, how natural a 0 or 1 is given the surrounding bits. Then he should divide the data into buckets (chosen randomly with the decryption key), require each bucket’s bits to XOR to the target ciphertext bit, and let the model pick the bit in each bucket whose probability is closest to 50 %—the safest one to flip. results.question: How do the shrines work in the semifinal version of Minpentai?
results.answer_fact: Every thousand turns, changes inside a shrine are XORed onto areas near its corners, then the shrine resets to a default rock.
results.answer_as_shown: The semifinal round adds five “shrines” – one in the board’s centre and one on each edge – that act as special cells that can change the board’s material. Every thousand turns the game takes whatever modifications players have made inside a shrine, applies them as an XOR operation to the four corner regions of that shrine, and then resets the shrine to a default rock formation [c14-b33]. Because XOR is reversible but not weight‑preserving, the shrines break ordinary mass‑conservation and cause the board to become increasingly full over time [c14-b35]. With resources cut to 20 % of normal, players use the shrines for “steering”: Zei positions a symbol‑carrying spaceship so a glider reaches a shrine at the right moment, turning it into an eternal glider factory that repeatedly spawns attacks [c14-b38].
